You are a data scientist at a long/short equity tech-focused hedge fund. You work with investors who understand technology well but do not have statistics or computer science backgrounds. Use whatever techniques are available to you, but make sure your work is interpretable by the investment staff rather than a black box.

You have a sandbox with Python and common data libraries, and the files attached to the request. The sandbox has no internet access. Today is 2018-11-03.

Predict JWN's quarterly full-price net sales from the transaction-sensor data.

Attached:
- `sensor_panel.csv`: daily transaction counts (`ct`) and dollar amounts (`amt`) by ticker and data source, through 2018-11-03. JWN appears as JWN_JWN.
- `data_brief.md`: the note that came with the data, describing the sensors.
- `actuals.csv`: JWN's reported full-price net sales (US department store / off-price retailer, fiscal quarters (fiscal year ends late January / early February)), in USD millions, from our data feed. It holds every value reported on or before 2018-11-03: FY2013 Q1 through FY2018 Q2, including figures re-reported in later filings, with the date each was reported.

FY2018 Q3 ended on 2018-11-03 and has not been reported yet. Provide in-sample estimates for the prior quarters and an out-of-sample estimate, with a range, for FY2018 Q3.

End your final message with:
1. A write-up for the investment staff, in markdown.
2. A fenced ```json block with exactly these fields:

```json
{"target_period": "FY2018 Q3", "unit": "USD millions",
 "point": 0, "low": 0, "high": 0, "interval_level": 0.9,
 "in_sample": [{"period_end": "YYYY-MM-DD", "estimate": 0}],
 "vs_consensus": "no_consensus"}
```

`low` and `high` bound your range at `interval_level` confidence. `in_sample` lists your estimate for each prior quarter you modeled.

[attached: sensor_panel.csv, actuals.csv, data_brief.md]

[stdout]

Anomaly Detection Exercise
Overview
Our investment process often starts with datasets that include a fair bit of signal but also significant noise. Attached is a very small (and partially simplified/derived) subset of data that counts the number of transactions and the amount spent per day at various companies/company segments as reported by four anonymized data sources. You can think of these data sources abstracted as ‘sensors’ that provide a timely read on underlying company trends, which may malfunction and provide poor reads at times.
We would like you to take this data and build a model that outputs a confidence score or probability for each datapoint that indicates where the data can be trusted or not trusted. Specifically, we are looking to cleanse the data of two types of potential issues:
Anomalous values: An individual datapoint can often be too low if a sensor doesn’t properly transmit the data, or too high for a variety of reasons (double counting/contamination/etc.).
Sudden level shifts across time: if a sensor changes the way it behaves, the read may be higher or lower persistently in perpetuity or for a period of time.
At this stage, there is no ‘ground truth’ or training data. But you can use past history or some notion of what is going on across timeseries to get a sense for what is normal.
Importantly, the model should not use foresight (i.e. data with future dates) to inform what is likely anomalous in the past. As such, the model should get better at divining confidence over time (though you may not be able to quantify, which is fine).
Data Description
Attached is an Excel file with two data-frames that contain the same data in two formats (one is pivoted for your convenience, but feel free not to use if you are just going to import flat tab).
Looking at the ‘flat’ tab:
Date is the day that a transaction occurred
Ct is the number of transactions the sensor reported
Amt is the dollar value of those transactions all added up
Ticker is either a company or in the case where an underline is present, a company segment (i.e., AAL is American Airlines while JWN_RACK is Nordstrom Rack)
Industry is self-explanatory. Note that we have only provided two here out of many that exist.
Source_id is a unique ID for each sensor. Note that there are only four provided here.
Guidance
Spend some time looking at the data before beginning. You will be able to see several instances of large data spikes and level shifts with the naked eye. Those are the types of items that we want to identify at scale (i.e. imagine you had to do this across hundreds more sensors and companies; the bar for the model is to identify those obviously wrong datapoints in an automated fashion).
Use whatever analytical tools and methods you are comfortable with. Learning a new language or technique is certainly not required. We tend to work in python, but use whatever is best for you.
Feel free to use any open-source packages that are helpful (but do let us know which you’ve chosen if any and why), or none at all.
Spend whatever time you think is required to get to a MVP output. This probably looks like a day, maybe two. We don’t expect you to ‘solve’ the problem fully (and to some extent the problem can’t be fully solved). We just want to see how you would approach the problem and what sort of scrappy results you can generate, while being cognizant of your time. Please keep track of your time so we know what you invested.
Simple is fine. Don’t feel the need to dazzle us with complexity if it isn’t immediately helpful.
Feel free to throw out any ‘junk’ data if it helps you (for instance, the leading portion of a sensor if there are very few transactions, but please do so programmatically within the model (so that your methodology could theoretically scale).
Necessary output is a confidence score for each datapoint. Better would be some notion of whether you believe a datapoint represents a point-anomaly or a level-shift. If you would like to produce a ‘clean’ version of each timeseries (i.e. removing or replacing an anomalous values, or adjusting a timeseries to remove the impact of a level-shift) that would be interesting for inspection, but is not required. Any means of clearly visualizing your output would also be helpful but is not required.
Ultimately, please deliver your output above, plus the code you used to generate the output in a reproduceable / interpretable format (this could be a notebook or just commented code). Presentation of the output need not be anything formal, but plan to chat through briefly afterwards to discuss your approach, what went well / not well, and what you would do with more time / etc. should complete the exercise.
Ask whatever questions you’d like, but note that we are purposely keeping the means of attack open-ended to see how you think about things.

exec(open('/tmp/load.py').read())
A=d.pivot_table(index='date',columns=['source_id','ticker'],values='amt').asfreq('D')
# --- Step 1: cross-source point anomaly cleaning for JWN_JWN ---
J=A.xs('JWN_JWN',axis=1,level=1)
# ratio to trailing 8-week same-weekday median (no foresight)
def base(s):
    out=pd.Series(np.nan,index=s.index)
    for w in range(7):
        x=s[s.index.dayofweek==w]
        out[x.index]=x.shift(1).rolling(8,min_periods=4).median()
    return out
R=np.log(J/J.apply(base))
cons=R.median(axis=1)  # cross-source consensus move (real events: holidays, Anniversary Sale)
dev=R.sub(cons,axis=0)
flag=(dev.abs()>np.log(1.8))
Jc=J.copy()
# replace flagged values by base*exp(consensus)
Jb=J.apply(base)
for s in J: 
    m=flag[s]; Jc.loc[m,s]=Jb.loc[m,s]*np.exp(cons[m])
EOF

cd /tmp; cat > /tmp/fit.py <<'EOF'
exec(open('/tmp/pipe.py').read())
import statsmodels.api as sm
def run(cols, data=M, label=''):
    m=data.dropna(subset=['act']).copy()
    x=m[cols].mean(axis=1); X=sm.add_constant(x)
    fit=sm.OLS(m.act,X).fit()
    # leave-one-out
    loo=[]
    for i in m.index:
        tr=m.drop(i); f=sm.OLS(tr.act,sm.add_constant(tr[cols].mean(axis=1))).fit()
        loo.append(m.act[i]-(f.params.iloc[0]+f.params.iloc[1]*x[i]))
    loo=pd.Series(loo,index=m.index)
    xq=data[cols].mean(axis=1).iloc[-1]
    print(f'{label:20s} {cols} a={fit.params.iloc[0]*100:.2f}% b={fit.params.iloc[1]:.2f} R2={fit.rsquared:.2f} resid_sd={np.sqrt(fit.scale)*100:.2f}% LOO_rmse={np.sqrt((loo**2).mean())*100:.2f}% xQ3={xq*100:.2f}% predQ3={(fit.params.iloc[0]+fit.params.iloc[1]*xq)*100:.2f}%')
    return fit,loo
if __name__=='__main__':
    for c in [['rel2'],['rel3'],['rel4'],['rel2','rel3','rel4'],['rel1','rel2','rel3','rel4']]:
        run(c)
    print('excluding FY18Q2:')
    for c in [['rel2','rel3','rel4'],['rel2','rel4']]:
        run(c,M.drop(pd.Timestamp('2018-08-04')))
EOF

I estimate JWN's FY2018 Q3 full-price net sales at **$2,082M**, with a 90% range of **$1,959M–$2,213M**. That is about 2.7% below what I think last year's Q3 becomes once restated on the new reporting basis (about $2,139M). The sensors help only modestly: the model is off by about 2.8% on average on quarters it didn't see, and simply rolling last year forward is not much worse.

## Write-up for the investment staff

### Approach
1. **Clean the daily data.** I flagged a day as a fault only when one sensor moved sharply but the other three didn't. Real events like Christmas closures, Easter or the Anniversary Sale open show up in all four sensors at once, so they were kept. For JWN, nearly all the flags were in Source 1, which is tiny (about 80 transactions a day) and noisy. Sources 2–4 were essentially clean.
2. **Use Nordstrom's exact fiscal-quarter dates.** I added up each sensor's dollars over the actual fiscal quarter boundaries. This automatically handles the 53-week FY2017 and the one-week calendar shift in FY2018.
3. **Remove sensor drift.** The raw sensors drift a lot over time. For example, Source 1 grew about 80% in 2017 for every company it covers, while Source 3 shrank about 10% in 2016. To correct this, I compared JWN's year-on-year growth with the typical (median) growth of the other 17 companies in the same sensor. JWN growing faster or slower than the rest of the panel is the signal.
4. **Turn the signal into a sales estimate.** I averaged that signal across Sources 2, 3 and 4 and fitted a simple line on 14 quarters (FY15 Q1 to FY18 Q2): reported growth ≈ 1.1% + 0.67 × (JWN growth minus panel growth). I left Source 1 out because it is too noisy.

### The FY2018 Q3 estimate
- **Sensor signal is weak:** JWN grew about 5.7% less than the panel (Source 2: −5.7%, Source 3: −3.9%, Source 4: −7.4%). The model turns that into about −2.7% year-on-year.
- **The weakness looks like Anniversary Sale timing, not demand.** In FY17 roughly the last week of the sale fell in Q3; in FY18 only about one day did. Leaving out the first two weeks of the quarter, raw sensor growth improves by about 4–5 points in every source.
- **The comparison base has to be restated.** In FY2018 JWN re-reported its prior-year quarters higher: Q1 FY17 rose 6.2% (2,030 → 2,156) and Q2 FY17 rose 5.3% (2,706 → 2,850). Restated Q3 FY17 hasn't been published yet. I assumed it rises by the average, 5.8%, to about $2,139M. My $2,082M is therefore on the new basis. It would look like **+3.0%** against the originally reported $2,022M, but that comparison mixes the two bases.
- **The range** reflects the model's errors on quarters it didn't see (3.4%, applied as roughly ±6% for 90% confidence) plus some uncertainty about the restatement.

### How well it fits (in-sample)
- **Typical error:** about 2.4% in-sample and 2.8% on quarters left out of the fit. Simply rolling forward last year's figure would miss by about 3.6%.
- **Biggest misses:** Q4 FY17 came in 4.6% above the estimate, and the model underestimated the extra 53rd week. Q2 FY18 came in 7.2% below the estimate: reported sales fell 5% on the restated basis while the sensors were flat to up.
- **FY2018 so far:** both new-basis quarters are among the misses (Q1 came in 3% above, Q2 7% below). Read them with caution.

### Risks
- **The new reporting basis is the main uncertainty.** Q2 FY18 shows sensor transactions and reported sales came apart this year.
- **Possible upside:** if orders placed online during the Anniversary Sale in late Q2 were counted as sales when shipped in early Q3, Q3 would come in higher than the sensors suggest.
- **Restatement size:** if restated Q3 FY17 rises 5.3% or 6.2% (the two FY17 precedents) instead of 5.8%, the estimate moves by about ±$10M.
